title: Management of the herd
competency: Describe housing, feeding, breeding, lactation and waste in dairy management.

keywords.def: A group of cattle kept together.
The secretion of milk from the mammary glands.
The pattern of lactation and pregnancy in a cow.
Harm to cattle from too much heat; it lowers fertility and milk.

en.text: Modern dairy farms group animals by age, needs and milk production. Housing must give feed, water and protection from heat and cold; heat stress lowers fertility and milk, and shade helps. Feed is the largest expense; diets depend on each animal's growth, milk and breeding status.

screens.title: Hot day
screens.ask: Cows stand in hot sun all day with no shade. What happens to their milk?
screens.after: Heat stress lowers fertility and milk production. Shade helps.

screens.title: 3.2.5 Management of the herd
paras: Dairy management changes with new technology and rules.
It covers nutrition, housing, health, reproduction and waste.
Farms divide animals into groups by age, needs and milk production.
The milking herd is managed most carefully.

screens.title: Housing systems
paras: Housing must give feed, water and protection from heat and cold.
Heat stress can lower fertility and milk production.
Shade is a common way to reduce heat stress. Barns may use fans.
Very cold weather can even kill cattle, so housing must be warm.

screens.title: Nutritional management
paras: Feed is the largest expense, whether grazing land or bought crops.
Rotational grazing is a common pasture method.
Diets differ by growth rate, milk production and breeding status.

screens.title: Key words
defs: A group of cattle kept together.
Harm to cattle from too much heat; it lowers fertility and milk.

opts: Feed, water and protection from bad weather
screens.ans: Feed, water and protection from bad weather

screens.text: Feed is the largest expense in raising cattle.
What is a common way to reduce heat stress?
screens.why: Shade is very common; barns may add fans.

screens.text: A farmer gives every cow the same feed: calves, milking cows and dry cows. What is wrong?
opts: Diets should differ by growth, milk production and breeding status
screens.ans: Diets should differ by growth, milk production and breeding status
screens.why: The book says diets must be prepared differently for each animal's needs.
screens.clue: Do all animals need the same food?

en.text: A cow gives milk only after she has a calf. Lactation is the secretion of milk from the mammary glands; it continues while the cow is milked but slowly falls. Farmers time breeding to keep milk high. Managed waste is an excellent fertilizer. Starting a dairy needs shelter, breeds, fodder, daily care, disease control and breeding management.

screens.title: Milk and calves
screens.ask: Can a cow give milk before she has ever had a calf?
screens.after: No. A cow produces milk only after giving birth.

screens.title: Reproductive and lactation management
paras: Female calves are raised to replace older cows.
A dairy cow's life is a cycle of pregnancy and lactation.
A cow will not produce milk until she has given birth.
Lactation is the secretion of milk from the mammary glands.

screens.title: The lactation cycle
paras: After a calf is born, the cow begins to lactate.
Milk continues while she is milked, but it steadily declines.
Farmers time the next breeding to get the most milk.
This pattern of lactation and pregnancy is the lactation cycle.

screens.title: Waste and starting a dairy farm
paras: Well-managed cattle waste is an excellent fertilizer.
It adds organic matter and improves soil.

screens.text: A farmer wants milk all year. Which plan fits the lactation cycle?
opts: Time each cow's breeding so new lactations start regularly
screens.ans: Time each cow's breeding so new lactations start regularly
screens.why: Milk only starts after calving and declines over time. Planned breeding restarts lactation and keeps milk coming.
